newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-Limited damage from Woods affair.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-Limited damage from Woods affair.

text.p: The damage from a political scandal depends on: (a) how weighty the allegations are and (b) how long it lasts.
Our concern is not what the government should or should not have done in the Woods affair. Rather, the question is: how does this affect the administration's standing with voters?
The answer is: probably not much, although the outcomes of these things are extremely difficult to predict.
The scandal contains two allegations that might damage the government.
Firstly, a very junior member of the government, the parliamentary secretary for health, is being investigated for fiddling his expenses, an allegation he denies.

The investigation itself may repel some voters -- and of course we have no firm way to calculate how many -- and if Woods is subsequently prosecuted and convicted then the government might lose a little more support.
Note, however, that he would be a former senator by the time of any prosecution, and that would mitigate the loss.

Secondly, the opposition asserts that Prime Minister John Howard has tried to keep the investigation under wraps and, moreover, misled the public when he failed to admit on television he had known about it for months.
Howard said he could not publicise the investigation since that would tip-off Woods.
As to the other accusation -- misleading the public -- he says he simply forgot.
The opposition might say this is an unsatisfactory response, and if so it might damage the government's support a little, but it is difficult to see where the affair goes from here.
If the opposition cannot come up with new developments to feed the media's need for a fresh angle then the story connecting Woods with Howard disappears.

Often a scandal damages a government not because of the original unattractive event -- in this case, the alleged expenses-fiddling -- but because of subsequent attempts to cover it up, which tend to keep it going.
Former health minister Carmen Lawrence's Easton affair comes to mind.
Perth solicitor Penny Easton killed herself after Lawrence's Western Australian state government targetted her in parliament.

Lawrence suffered prolonged political damage in 1995 not because of her association with the suicide but because she denied knowing about it. An inquiry found that she did know about it and so the opposition could call her a liar.
In this case, it is difficult to see what further progress the opposition can make in accusing the government of a cover-up.
